meta.titre: Longitude and Time Zones: from degrees to hours and across the Date Line
meta.sous_theme: Calculating time and longitude, standard time and the International Date Line

sections.contenu_markdown: A family in Yaoundé wants to telephone a cousin who studies in North America. If they call at eight in the evening, will the cousin be awake, or asleep in the middle of the night? The answer depends on how far west the cousin lives, that is, on longitude. The GCE tests this with short calculations of time and longitude, with questions on why some countries have several time zones, and with the effect of crossing the International Date Line. These marks are won by following the same few steps every time.

items: Lines of longitude (meridians) run from the North Pole to the South Pole, and lines of latitude run east to west.
The earth turns once on its axis in 24 hours, from west to east.
A full circle has 360 degrees, and 1 hour has 60 minutes.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Longitude

**Longitude** is the angular distance of a place east or west of the **Prime Meridian**, which is 0° and passes through Greenwich in London. It is measured from 0° to 180° east and from 0° to 180° west. **GMT** (Greenwich Mean Time) is the time at the Prime Meridian.

### Degrees and hours

The earth turns through 360° in 24 hours, so it turns through 360 ÷ 24 = **15° every hour**, and therefore through 1° every 4 minutes.

| Longitude difference | Time difference |
|---|---|
| 15° | 1 hour |
| 1° | 4 minutes |
| 360° | 24 hours |

The earth turns from west to east, so the sun reaches places in the east first. A place **east** of Greenwich is **ahead** of GMT (its time is later), and a place **west** is **behind** GMT. A short rule is "east, more; west, less".

- Time east of Greenwich: local time = GMT + (longitude ÷ 15) hours.
- Time west of Greenwich: local time = GMT - (longitude ÷ 15) hours.

### Standard time and time zones

If every town used its own local time, clocks would differ from one town to the next. Each country therefore chooses a **standard time** for the whole country, based on a central meridian. The world is divided into 24 time zones, each about 15° wide. A country with a large east-west extent, such as Russia or the USA, has several time zones, because its east and west are many hours apart. Cameroon extends over only a few degrees of longitude, so it uses a single standard time, one hour ahead of GMT.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When local time and GMT are both given
variantes.contenu_markdown: 1) Subtract to find the time difference. 2) Multiply the hours by 15 to get degrees. 3) If local time is ahead of GMT, the place is east; if behind, it is west. Add minutes carefully: 20 minutes is 5°.

variantes.nom: Finding the time at a second place
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the time at one place and the longitudes of two places are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Convert the first time to GMT, using the first longitude. Then convert GMT to the second place using its longitude. If the two places are on opposite sides of Greenwich, add their longitudes to find the difference; on the same side, subtract.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a traveller or a time calculation crosses 180°
variantes.contenu_markdown: The International Date Line follows roughly the 180° meridian and bends to avoid dividing countries. A traveller crossing it **westwards** (for example from America towards Asia) moves the calendar **forward one day**; crossing it **eastwards** (from Asia towards America) moves the calendar **back one day**. The clock time does not change at the line.

sections.enonce_markdown: At town P the local time is 2:00 pm on Thursday when GMT is 9:00 am on the same day. (a) Find the longitude of P. (b) Find the time and day at town Q, on longitude 120° W, at that moment.

etapes.justification: The difference between local time and GMT is the time difference between P and Greenwich.
P's local time is ahead of GMT, so the sun reached P before Greenwich.

etapes.action: Convert Q's longitude to a time difference.
etapes.justification: 120° ÷ 15° per hour gives the hours, and the west is behind GMT.
Take Thursday 9:00 am and go back 8 hours; check whether the day changes.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) Town P is on longitude **75° E**. (b) At the same moment it is **1:00 am on Thursday** at Q (120° W).

items.erreur_markdown: "Town P is on 75° E, so its clocks are 75 hours ahead of GMT."
items.pourquoi_faux: One hour corresponds to 15°, not 1°. The degrees must be divided by 15.

items.erreur_markdown: Subtracting hours for a place in the east and adding hours for a place in the west.
items.pourquoi_faux: The earth turns from west to east, so places in the east are ahead and places in the west are behind.

items.erreur_markdown: "The difference between 30° E and 45° W is 15°."
items.pourquoi_faux: The two places are on opposite sides of the Prime Meridian, so the degrees must be added.

items.erreur_markdown: "Russia and the USA have several time zones because they are large countries."
items.pourquoi_faux: Size from north to south does not change the time. Only the extent from east to west matters.
items.correction_markdown: They stretch over **many degrees of longitude**, so their eastern and western parts are hours apart.

items.erreur_markdown: Forgetting to change the day when the calculation passes midnight or crosses the Date Line.
items.pourquoi_faux: A time before 12 midnight or after it belongs to a different date.
items.correction_markdown: After each subtraction or addition, check whether you moved to the previous or the next day.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) What is the local time at a town on longitude 45° E when GMT is 12 noon? (b) What is the local time at a town on longitude 30° W when GMT is 6:00 pm?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) 45 ÷ 15 = 3 hours; east is ahead, so 12 noon + 3 h = **3:00 pm**.

(b) 30 ÷ 15 = 2 hours; west is behind, so 6:00 pm - 2 h = **4:00 pm**.

items.enonce_markdown: Town A is on longitude 75° E and town B is on longitude 30° W. At 3:00 pm on Monday at A, (a) what is the time at B? (b) A flight leaves A at that moment and takes 6 hours to reach B. What is the local time and day of arrival at B?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A and B are on opposite sides of Greenwich, so the difference is 75 + 30 = 105°, which is 105 ÷ 15 = 7 hours. B is west of A, so B is behind: 3:00 pm - 7 h = **8:00 am on Monday**.

(b) Arrival time at B = 8:00 am + 6 h = **2:00 pm on Monday** (local time at B).

items.enonce_markdown: Town X is on longitude 170° E and town Y is on longitude 170° W. At 6:00 pm on Monday at X, what are the time and day at Y? Explain why the two towns, which are only 20° of longitude apart, have different days.
items.solution_markdown:
170 ÷ 15 = 11 h 20 min.

GMT: X is east, so GMT = 6:00 pm - 11 h 20 min = 6:40 am on Monday.

Y is west, so Y = 6:40 am - 11 h 20 min = 7:20 pm on **Sunday**.

**Answer: 7:20 pm on Sunday.** X is just west of the International Date Line and Y is just east of it. Between them the calendar changes by one day (a traveller going from X eastwards to Y moves the calendar back one day), although only about one hour and twenty minutes of clock time separate them.

items_markdown: Longitude is measured east or west of the Prime Meridian (0°, through Greenwich), from 0° to 180°.
15° of longitude equal 1 hour, and 1° equals 4 minutes.
East of Greenwich the time is ahead of GMT (add); west of Greenwich it is behind (subtract).
To find longitude: time difference × 15, with ahead meaning east and behind meaning west.
Countries with a large east-west extent, such as Russia and the USA, have several time zones; Cameroon has one, one hour ahead of GMT.
Crossing the International Date Line westwards adds a day; crossing it eastwards takes a day away.
